core_obligations: Reduce to K equal to the separable algebraic closure of k by observing that base change along the separable closures is a bijection on irreducible components (proof lines 1637-1651).

Show the image of an irreducible component of X_K is an irreducible component of X: flatness makes generic points descend through the projection, integrality makes the image closed, and a closed irreducible subset containing the generic point of a component is that component (proof lines 1654-1664).
Get surjectivity: for a component T of X the inverse image is a nonempty union of components of X_K, and each of them maps onto T by the first part (proof lines 1665-1669).
proof_roadmap: Reduce to the separable closure (proof lines 1637-1651).
Use flatness and integrality to identify the image of a component (proof lines 1654-1664).
difficulty_reason: For an extension of fields K/k and a scheme X over k, the lemma shows that the image of every irreducible component of X_K is an irreducible component of X, so that there is a canonical surjective map on sets of irreducible components (statement lines 1621-1634). The proof first reduces to the case where K is the separable closure of k by using that the base change along separable algebraic closures induces a bijection on irreducible components (proof lines 1637-1651). The main step then uses the two structural properties of the projection: flatness makes generalizations lift, so generic points of components of the base change map to generic points of components of X, and integrality makes the projection universally closed, so the image of a component is closed; an irreducible closed subset containing a generic point of a component is that component (proof lines 1654-1664). Surjectivity is then read off from the fact that the inverse image of a component of X is a nonempty union of components of X_K, each of which maps onto it by the first part (proof lines 1665-1669). The claim is H2: a schematic reduction plus a two-property argument, with the correct combination of flatness and integrality being the point.
